profile.summary: James is a pastoral letter addressed to Jewish Christians scattered throughout the diaspora, pressured by poverty, injustice, and hostility because of faith in Jesus. Its purpose is to call God's people to a mature, complete and coherent faith that does not limit itself to verbal confession, but appears in concrete attitudes, especially in the way of living with God and with others. The book integrates practical wisdom, ethical exhortation and strong echo of Jesus" teaching, insisting that true fidelity endures trials, rejects partiality, dominates the language, seeks the wisdom of God and lives in humility before the Lord.
profile.setting: The letter was most likely written by James, brother of Jesus, who became a recognized leader of the church of Jerusalem after the resurrection. Authorship is traditionally attributed to it, and the source presents this identification as the most likely. The date is also debated, but the suggested scenario is that of a very ancient composition, possibly between persecution under Herod Agrippa and the council of Jerusalem, when the separation between synagogue and church could still be described in a fluid way. The recipients were Jewish Christians scattered among the Jewish communities of the diaspora in the Greco-Roman world, living under economic, social and religious pressure. The letter's environment shows knowledge of situations typical of Palestine and the Jewish world scattered throughout the empire, and the text combines language of wisdom, prophetic exhortation and very direct pastoral appeals.

structure.label: Proofing, wisdom and faith
structure.description: The openness presents the perspective of the letter: to face trials with perseverance, to ask for wisdom from God and to receive with meekness the word that produces practical obedience.

structure.label: Listen and practice; faith without partiality
structure.description: James contrasts the mere listening with the practice of the word and applies this to community life, especially in the treatment without favoritism and in the relationship between faith and works.

structure.label: The language and wisdom from above
structure.description: The chapter focuses on the use of speech, warning about the destructive power of the tongue and showing that true wisdom is recognized for its fruits of peace and purity.

structure.label: Submission to God and criticism of arrogance
structure.description: The chapter confronts disorderly desires, friendship with the world and presumption in human planning, calling for repentance, humility and submission to the Lord.

structure.label: End comfort, patience and mutual care
structure.description: The conclusion denounces unjust oppression, strengthens believers for the patient waiting for the Lord's coming and closes with exhortations to prayer, community care and restoration of those who deviate.

themes: Perseverance in the middle of the trial
Humility before God and Peaceful Community Life
readingKeys: Notice how the letter links doctrine and practice: almost every instruction leads to concrete behavior.
Realize the frequent contrasts between appearance and reality: listening and doing, wealth and oppression, wisdom of high and earthly wisdom.
Read the letter as a pastoral exhortation to a pressed community, noting how James treats prayer, language, justice and humility as marks of true faith.
profile.cautions: The introduction is based on the traditional assignment to James, brother of Jesus, but recognizes that the exact date is not certain; the most likely picture is that of a very ancient letter prior to the Jerusalem council. It is also important to read the emphasis on works within the context of the letter: James does not teach salvation by merit, but states that works are the necessary evidence of a real faith.

dossier.narratedEra: The letter is located in the Jewish world of diaspora in the 1st century, with Jewish-Christian readers scattered outside Palestine and living under social and economic pressure in communities of the Greco-Roman environment. The immediate narrative background includes the Jerusalem church led by James, the brother of Jesus, and a Christian community still very close to Jewish vocabulary and institutions.
dossier.compositionEra: The sources place the composition probably at the beginning of the church's history, possibly in the 1940s, after the persecution of Herod Agrippa (AD 44) and before the council of Jerusalem (c. AD 49-50), although a source highlights that the exact date is uncertain. The traditional authorship is attributed to James, brother of Jesus; a source identifies him as the son of Alphaeus and the apostle, while another describes him as Jesus" brother and recognized leader of the church of Jerusalem. There is also mention of wide public reading in early churches.

politics.title: Persecution that dispersed readers
politics.detail: Readers are linked to the dispersion caused by the persecution that began with Stephen's death and who struck Jewish Christians outside Judea.
politics.readingImpact: The letter does not speak to a stable and privileged community, but to displaced believers, vulnerable and under pressure, which helps to read the exhortations to perseverance, patience and integrity as concrete pastoral responses.

politics.title: Herod Agrippa and the initial chronological window
politics.detail: The letter is located after the persecution under Herod Agrippa, mentioned as a landmark around A.D. 44, and before the council of Jerusalem.
politics.readingImpact: This reinforces the reading of James as written at an early stage of the Christian controversy, before the most developed disputes over the Gentile inclusion and before certain later theological formulations.

politics.title: Greco-Roman Empire as Jewish circulation space
politics.detail: The sources claim that in the middle of the first century there were Jewish communities throughout the Greco-Roman world, with Jews traveling widely through these empires.
politics.readingImpact: The scenario explains why James can treat his readers as part of a scattered diaspora and why his exhortation needs to function in diverse social contexts, not just in Jerusalem.

politics.title: Conflict with oppressive elites
politics.detail: The poor readers suffered economic oppression and abuse because of faith in Jesus; in addition, the letter denounces rich people who exploit workers and drag believers into the courts.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of warnings against favoritism, unjust wealth and exploitation gains social weight: James speaks of real inequality, not mere moral abstraction.

politics.title: Jerusalem as a Probable Place of Writing
politics.detail: The location in Jerusalem is inferred from Acts and Galatians, who place James there as leader of the church.
politics.readingImpact: If written from Jerusalem, the letter gains closeness to the center of the early Jewish-Christian leadership and a still strongly Jewish environment, which helps to understand the tone of continuity with Israel.

customs.title: Christian meetings called synagogue
customs.detail: The sources note that, at an early stage, the church meeting could be called a synagogue, in a seemingly non-technical use of "church."
customs.readingImpact: This shows that James writes in an environment in which the institutional boundaries between Judaism and Christianity still appear fluid, which affects the reading of Tg 2:2 and 5:14.

customs.title: Public reading of the Scriptures
customs.detail: As few people could read and the manuscripts were not easily available, reading the Scriptures in public worship was important.
customs.readingImpact: This reinforces the community character of the epistle: James was made to be heard in assembly, and his emphasis on practicing the word gains oral and liturgical strength.

customs.title: Vulnerability of orphans and widows
customs.detail: Orphans and widows are described as the most defenseless members of ancient society, dependent on care of others because of the absence of the male provider.
customs.readingImpact: The "pura" religion in Tg 1:27 should be read as concrete social care, not only inner devotion; the ethics of James includes assistance to the helpless.

customs.title: Work and harvest
customs.detail: The rich of Tg 5 are depicted as exploitative owners who retain salary of diarist workers used in the harvest.
customs.readingImpact: The complaint against the rich is not generic: it presupposes an unequal rural economy, in which workers depended on fair payment and could be injured judicially.

customs.title: Anointing with oil and local leadership
customs.detail: In Tg 5:14, priests of the congregation are called to pray and anoint the sick with oil, a gesture associated with divine blessing and healing.
customs.readingImpact: The passage shows a community practice of spiritual and physical care, in which prayer, local authority and visible sign go together.

customs.title: Dinners, injustice and community orality
customs.detail: The letter mentions severe verbal conflicts, oaths, maledicence and blessing/corruption by speech, suggesting community life marked by internal tensions.
customs.readingImpact: Exhortations about language and oaths sound like correction of daily speaking habits in a group that meets, debate and relates under pressure.

language.title: The Twelve Tribes and Continuity with Israel
language.detail: James 1:1 is read as an affirmation of the continuity of the Christian faith with the inheritance of Israel; the Twelve tribes evoke the restoration and meeting of the scattered people.
language.readingImpact: The reader is led to listen to the letter as a language of biblical identity, not as a rupture with Israel, reinforcing the continuity of the covenant's history.

language.title: Double allegiance and "divided heart"
language.detail: The language of Tg 1:6, 1:8 is explained as divided loyalty between God and the world; the usual translation "duvidar" is treated as insufficient to capture the meaning.
language.readingImpact: The central question is not only intellectual hesitation, but fractured fidelity; this shapes the whole letter as called spiritual integrity.

language.title: Rhetoric of diatribe and rhetorical questions
language.detail: The note identifies the use of diatribe in Tg 1:13 and several rhetorical questions, with an imaginary opponent being refuted.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that James not only instructs; he debates, anticipates objections and confronts moral self-justifications.

language.title: Agricultural, marine and climatic images of Palestine
language.detail: The notes point to allusions to scorching heat, brackish springs, cultivation of figs, olive trees and vines, the sea, and rains temporan and serodia.
language.readingImpact: These images link the letter to the Palestinian environment and make the illustrations more concrete: the reader imagines a rural and agricultural reality when receiving spiritual instructions.

language.title: Language, brake and poison
language.detail: The tongue is described with strong images: brake on horse, fire, world of iniquity, Gehenna and deadly poison, with possible allusion to the serpent of Eden.
language.readingImpact: Human speech is treated as a decisive spiritual and community force, capable of blessing or destroying; this extends the gravity of warnings about verbal conflicts.

language.title: Wisdom "high "high in contrast to "terrestrial' wisdom."
language.detail: Wisdom in James is not mere intellectual ability; it is practical discernment and moral purity, opposite of envy, selfish ambition, and demonic wisdom.
language.readingImpact: The text should be read as ethical and spiritual wisdom for community life, not as abstract information.

timeline.title: Assyrian squarence and Babylonian exile as remote origin of the diaspora
timeline.detail: The diaspora is connected to the scatters of Israel in the 8th century BC and Judah in 586 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: James speaks to a people whose dispersion has long roots; the identity of exiles helps to explain the language of dispersion and hope of restoration.

timeline.title: Christian Dispersion after Stephen
timeline.detail: The letter is linked to the dispersion of the Jewish-Christians caused by the persecution initiated with the stoning of Stephen.
timeline.readingImpact: This places the community in a moment of forced displacement and recent suffering, which gives urgency to the exhortations on perseverance.

timeline.title: James becomes leader of Jerusalem after the resurrection
timeline.detail: The sources claim that James, brother of Jesus, became a recognized leader of the church of Jerusalem shortly after the resurrection, with an echo of Acts 15 and 21.
timeline.readingImpact: The authority of the letter is understood in the light of a royal apostolic and pastoral leadership, rooted in the mother-in-mighth community of Christianity.

timeline.title: Persecution under Herod Agrippa and probable date of the letter
timeline.detail: One source places the wording after AD 44 and before AD 49-50; another only says that the date is uncertain.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should avoid rigid chronologies and read the epistle as a testimony of an early stage, prior to the large clashes on Gentiles.

timeline.title: Council of Jerusalem as a later chronological limit
timeline.detail: The letter is placed before the council dealing with the circumcision of Gentiles and the relationship between Gentiles and the Mosaic law.
timeline.readingImpact: This helps to understand why James still uses such Jewish language and why the letter does not discuss in detail the later Gentile conflict.

timeline.title: Growth of Gentile and Jewish communities in the Greco-Roman world
timeline.detail: The notes suggest a period in which Jews and Jewish Christians were already widely distributed throughout the cities of the empire, with established communities until the middle of the first century.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter can be read as an intervention in a scattered network of churches and synagogues, not just as a local message from Jerusalem.

investigation: The traditional authorship is attributed to James, brother of Jesus; one source also identifies him with James son of Alphaeus and treats him as one of the Twelve, while another emphasizes his fraternal relationship with Jesus and his leadership in Jerusalem.
The dating is presented as probable, not closed: one source favors AD 44-49/50, but another declares that the time of writing is uncertain.
The expression "twelve tribes" is treated by the sources as a language of continuity with Israel and hope of meeting, not as an indication of a closed ethnic group in a modern sociological sense.
The note on "sinagoga" in Tg 2:2 and "church" in Tg 5:14 shows a still fluid vocabulary between Judaism and early Christianity.
The section on the rich of Tg 5:1-6 describes concrete economic exploitation, but does not accurately identify which specific elites are in view; the application remains general within the text.
The sources highlight many literary and rhetorical elements, but do not intend to thoroughly reconstruct the historical genre of the letter; part of the interpretation is pastoral and intertextual.
There are mentions parallel to Matthew and Luke, but without pretense strict chronological dependence beyond what the notes explicitly say.

This dossier depends solely on the introductions and notes provided by Tyndale and Matthew Henry; therefore, it only includes explicitly stated or inferred data on them. There have been no gaps with external knowledge, and several questions remain debated, especially the exact date and accurate identification of traditional authorship. The notes well cover the Jewish context, the diaspora, poverty, speech and ethics, but offer less information about concrete imperial policy, detailed domestic life and fine chronologies. Some historical references appear only as an interpretive background, not as independent proof. Where there was inference, this was signaled as an interpretation; where there is divergence or uncertainty, this was indicated as debated.
